label: S1 E1
videoTitle: Phineas and Ferb First Episode | Rollercoaster | S1 E1 | Full Episode (Disney Channel Animation)
sources: Timing: official Disney Channel Animation upload on YouTube (video fLWBx37eKBM), timed English captions
Wording and speakers: Phineas and Ferb Wiki (Fandom) transcripts for Rollercoaster and Candace Loses Her Head
notes: Every clip gets 0.5 s extra at the start and 1 s at the end (clipPadding), because caption times run ahead of the audio.
YouTube captions are ALL CAPS and split into chunks, so clip ends are set at the next caption chunk. Some clips include one extra line at the end.
Caption fixes: at 2:19 Candace is talking to Stacy (captions say "CeCe"). At 12:46 Phineas says "a better one than Ferb" (captions say "that"). At 21:58 Ferb, not Phineas, says the gorilla line.
Two items come from songs (marked Sung). They are good for meaning but not ideal for everyday pronunciation.

lines: I, for one, am starting to get bored, and boredom is something up with which I will not put.
clips.hl: up with which I will not put

plain: Normal way: "Boredom is something I will not put up with."
Add "which": "Boredom is something which I will not put up with."
Move "up with" to the front of "which": "Boredom is something up with which I will not put."
Same meaning, just back to front. Nobody really talks like this. That's the joke.
expressions.meaning: "Put up with" = accept something annoying, without complaining. So the whole line means: "I'm getting bored, and I refuse to accept being bored." Some people say you shouldn't end a sentence with a little word like "with". Phineas follows that "rule" so strictly that the sentence sounds silly. It's a famous old joke, often credited to Winston Churchill.
expressions.listen: "I, for one" means "me, personally". Phineas says it like a speech.
expressions.example: I won't put up with my brother taking my Lego without asking.
expressions.practice: Someone keeps kicking the back of your seat in the car. Tell them you won't accept it.
expressions.tone: Playful and show-offy. In real life, use the normal way: "I won't put up with ___."

toneCards.situation: Announce to your family, like a king, that you will not be bored this summer.
toneCards.note: The back-to-front version is only for jokes.

toneCards.situation: Your brother keeps taking your Lego. "I won't put up with this!"
toneCards.note: The normal way. You mean it.

clips.label: Candace, to Mom
lines: What about the Mt. Rushmore bobblehead?

expressions.meaning: Boring, disappointing, not cool.
expressions.tone: Casual. Saying it about a ride is fine. Saying it about a gift someone offers you (like Candace) sounds rude.
expressions.listen: "Man," at the start is a sigh word. It shows Phineas is disappointed.
expressions.example: The playground is closed today? Lame.
expressions.practice: Your friend tells you the swimming pool is closed for cleaning all week.

toneCards.situation: The fireworks show is cancelled because of rain.
Grandma gives you a sweater she knitted.
toneCards.note: Don't call a gift lame. It hurts feelings. Try: "Thanks! It's not really my style."

toneCards.situation: Your friend tells a really bad joke.
toneCards.note: Friends say it with a smile.

lines: Why, if I built a rollercoaster, I would— That's it! I know what we're gonna do today.
Phineas, Ferb, I'm gonna go pick up a few things. You boys stay out of trouble, OK?

expressions.meaning: "I've got the idea!" You say it the moment a plan pops into your head.
expressions.listen: "Why," at the start is not a question. It's a surprised filler word. "Gonna" = going to.
expressions.example: That's it! Let's build a fort with the sofa cushions.
expressions.practice: You and your teacher can't decide what game to play. Suddenly you have an idea.

toneCards.situation: You suddenly know how to get your kite out of the tree.
You lose the same game for the fifth time. "That's it! I'm done!"
toneCards.note: A different meaning: I've had enough.

lines: Phineas, Ferb, I'm gonna go pick up a few things. You boys stay out of trouble, OK?

expressions.meaning: Don't do anything naughty while I'm away. The joke: the boys say "OK" and then build a giant rollercoaster.
expressions.example: Grandma said, "Stay out of trouble," so we just read comics. Mostly.
expressions.practice: You're leaving your little cousin with a babysitter for an hour. What do you say to them?

toneCards.situation: You're leaving your little cousin with Grandma for an hour.
Your friend who loves pranks is going to a sleepover.

clips.label: Candace checks with Mom
lines: I'm in charge, right? You did tell them I'm in charge?
Relax, Candace. Nobody has to be in charge.

clips.label: Candace announces it
lines: Mom says I'm in charge, conditionally.

clips.label: Candace shouts it again
lines: That's cool. You wait till the last minute, then.
Well, I'm watching you. And I'm in charge. Conditionally!

expressions.meaning: "In charge" = the boss, the person responsible. "Conditionally" = only if something happens. Mom said Candace is in charge only if a satellite crashes into the house. So she's not really in charge.
expressions.tone: Candace keeps adding "conditionally" because it's true, and it annoys her.
expressions.example: When Mom and Dad go out, my big cousin is in charge.
expressions.practice: Your teacher steps out for five minutes and asks you to watch the class. Tell your classmates.

toneCards.situation: Your teacher made you class monitor for the day.
Your little cousin is scared at the playground. "Don't worry, I'm in charge. I'll help you."
You're only in charge if the babysitter is late. Tell your friend, grumpily.

lines: Mom says I'm in charge, conditionally.

expressions.meaning: "I don't really care." Phineas isn't upset. He just doesn't care who's in charge.
expressions.tone: Said lightly, it's relaxed. Said with an eye-roll to a grown-up, it's rude.
expressions.example: You want the blue cup? Whatever, I'll take the red one.
expressions.practice: Your friend says, "I'm going first because I'm older." You don't mind.

toneCards.situation: Your friend asks: blue cup or red cup? You really don't mind.
Mom asks you to tidy your room, and you roll your eyes.
toneCards.note: With grown-ups, this sounds very rude.

lines: Wait a minute. What are you doing?
That's cool. You wait till the last minute, then.

expressions.meaning: To leave something until the latest possible time. Phineas is teasing Candace: she leaves her homework until the end of summer.
expressions.tone: Polite words, cheeky meaning.
expressions.listen: "Till" = until. "Wait a minute" (Candace) means "Hold on, something's strange."
expressions.example: I waited till the last minute to pack, so I forgot my swimsuit.
expressions.practice: Your friend hasn't started their school project, and it's due tomorrow.

toneCards.situation: Your sister says she'll start her holiday homework "later".
Your project is due tomorrow and you haven't started.
toneCards.note: "I left it till the last minute!"

lines: That's cool. You wait till the last minute, then.
Well, I'm watching you. And I'm in charge. Conditionally!

expressions.meaning: A warning: "I'm keeping an eye on you, so don't do anything bad."
expressions.tone: A playful threat. Friends say it as a joke.
expressions.example: That's my last cookie. I'm watching you!
expressions.practice: Your little cousin keeps creeping toward your snack.

toneCards.situation: Your cousin keeps creeping toward your last cookie.
Your friend promised not to cheat at cards this time.

lines: No, no, he's the cute one that works at Mr. Slushy Burger. Yeah, he totally smiled at me the last time I was there. I just about died.

expressions.meaning: "I almost died" from excitement or embarrassment. A big exaggeration. "Just about" = almost.
expressions.listen: "Totally" = completely. Very common slang, especially with teens.
expressions.example: My favorite footballer waved at me. I just about died!
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about a time you were super excited or super embarrassed.

toneCards.situation: Your favorite footballer waved at you.
You waved back at someone, but they were waving at the person behind you.

lines: Yeah, and they never get into trouble because Mom never catches them. One of these days, though, I'm gonna see to it that she catches them red-handed.

expressions.meaning: To catch someone while they're doing something wrong. This is Candace's goal in every episode.
expressions.listen: "One of these days" = some day soon (said with determination). "See to it that" = make sure that.
expressions.example: Dad caught my brother red-handed, with chocolate all over his face.
expressions.practice: Someone keeps eating your snacks. Tell your friend your plan.

toneCards.situation: You've set a trap to find out who keeps eating your snacks.
Dad found the dog with your sock in its mouth.

lines: Will you hold it down! I am trying to use the phone!

expressions.plain: Will you hold it down! = Please be quieter!
expressions.meaning: Be quieter!
expressions.tone: "Will you…!" looks like a question, but it's an annoyed command.
expressions.example: Hold it down, guys. Grandma's taking a nap.
expressions.practice: You're on a video call and everyone around you is being super loud.

toneCards.situation: You're on the phone and everyone is yelling.
The baby is sleeping. "Could you hold it down a bit?"
toneCards.note: "Could you… a bit?" makes it polite.

lines: Mom left me in charge, so there will be no shenanigans today.

expressions.meaning: "Shenanigans" = silly, naughty tricks. A fun word adults use when they're half-joking.
expressions.listen: Stress: she-NAN-i-gans.
expressions.example: OK team, no shenanigans on the bus, please.
expressions.practice: You're the captain of your team for a game. Set the rules.

toneCards.situation: You're team captain on the school bus.
Pretend to be Grandpa, smiling at kids being silly: "What shenanigans are you up to?"

clips.label: The first threat
lines: Ooh, I'm gonna go tell Mom, and when she sees what you are doing, you are going down! Down, down, down! D-O-W-N! Down!

expressions.meaning: "You're going to be in big trouble." In games, it means "I'm going to beat you."
expressions.tone: Threatening, but cartoon-style and over the top. Between friends before a game, it's fun trash talk, not mean.
expressions.listen: She spells it out, "D-O-W-N!", to make it extra dramatic.
expressions.example: Rematch at Mario Kart? You're going down!
expressions.practice: Your friend challenges you to a race to the swings.

toneCards.situation: Before a Mario Kart race with your friend.
You catch your brother breaking your favorite toy.

expressions.plain: What are you doing? → Whatcha doin'?
expressions.meaning: "What are you doing?" said fast and friendly. It's Isabella's catchphrase.
expressions.listen: "Whatcha" = what are you, said as one word: WUT-chuh. "Doin'" drops the g.
expressions.example: Hey Dad, whatcha doin'? Can I help?
expressions.practice: You walk into the kitchen and see Grandma mixing something in a big bowl.

toneCards.situation: You see Dad fixing his bike.
Your brother is standing next to your schoolbag, looking guilty.

lines: Wow. Isn't that kind of impossible?

expressions.meaning: "Some people might think so." A cool, calm answer that means: I'm doing it anyway.
expressions.listen: "Kind of impossible": "kind of" makes Isabella's question softer and more polite.
expressions.example: "Reading ten books this summer is crazy!" "Some might say."
expressions.practice: Someone says your plan to learn ten new magic tricks this week is impossible.

toneCards.situation: "Reading ten books this summer is impossible!"
Your friend says, "You're the best swimmer in our class."

lines: Hey, Ferb. Does your stepbrother ever talk?
Ferb? He's more of a man of action.

expressions.meaning: Someone who does things instead of talking about them. It's funny because Ferb hardly ever speaks.
expressions.example: My sister doesn't say much, but she's more of a woman of action.
expressions.practice: Describe a friend who's quiet but great at building or sports.

toneCards.situation: Your friend fixed the broken swing without saying a word.
Your friend never talks in group chats but always shows up.

lines: I was gonna go to the pool. You want to go swimming?
Kind of in the middle of something here.
Oh. Right. OK. I'll see you later, then.

expressions.plain: I'm kind of in the middle of something. = I'm busy right now.
expressions.meaning: "I'm busy right now." A polite way to say no.
expressions.tone: Isabella's "Oh. Right. OK." shows she's a little disappointed.
expressions.listen: Phineas drops the start. The full sentence is "I'm kind of in the middle of something here."
expressions.example: Can I call you back? I'm kind of in the middle of something.
expressions.practice: Your friend asks you to play right when you're finishing a puzzle.

toneCards.situation: Your friend calls while you're finishing a puzzle.
Your sister interrupts you for the fifth time.

clips.label: up to his old tricks
lines: Good morning, Agent P. The evil Dr. Doofenshmirtz is up to his old tricks. … I want you to get over to his hideout right away, find out what he's up to, and put a stop to it.

clips.label: up to no good
lines: Good morning, Agent P. Dr. Doofenshmirtz is up to no good again.

clips.label: what those two are up to
lines: Wait till you see what those two are up to.

expressions.meaning: "Up to something" = doing something, often secret or naughty. "Up to his old tricks" = doing the same bad things again. "Up to no good" = doing something bad.
expressions.example: My brothers are way too quiet. They're up to something.
expressions.practice: You hear giggling from the next room, and then total silence.

toneCards.situation: Your siblings are giggling, then suddenly silent.
Ask a friend about their weekend plans: "What are you up to this weekend?"
toneCards.note: Here it just means: what are you doing? Nothing naughty.

lines: As always, Agent P, it is imperative that your cover identity as a mindless domestic pet remains intact. Now get out there. We're all counting on you.

expressions.meaning: "We trust you and need you to do this."
expressions.listen: "It is imperative" is very formal. It means "it is very important."
expressions.example: You're our goalkeeper today. We're all counting on you!
expressions.practice: Your friend is the last runner in the relay race.

toneCards.situation: Your friend is the last runner in the relay.
You're the last runner. "Everyone's counting on me…"

expressions.phrase: the way I see it / kick in

lines: So the way I see it, the solid fuel rockets kick in in the mall parking lot. Then we release the snakes during the corkscrew around the interstate.

expressions.meaning: "Kick in" = start working. "The way I see it" = in my opinion, here's my plan.
expressions.example: The way I see it, we need more tape. Then the wings kick in when we throw it.
expressions.practice: Explain your plan for winning a paper airplane contest. Start with "The way I see it…"

toneCards.situation: Explain how your paper rocket's rubber band kicks in.
After a long day at the beach: "I think the tiredness is kicking in."

expressions.phrase: It seems like we've had this conversation before.

lines: Did a satellite crash into the house?
No, no, no! You gotta see what Phineas and Ferb are doing.
It seems like we've had this conversation before.
clips.hl: It seems like we've had this conversation before.

expressions.meaning: "You've told me this before, and it wasn't true."
expressions.tone: Dry and tired, with a little teasing.
expressions.example: "I'll tidy my room after this game." "Hmm. It seems like we've had this conversation before."
expressions.practice: Your friend promises, again, to give your book back tomorrow.

toneCards.situation: Your brother says, again, that he'll tidy up "right after this game".
Your friend forgot to return your book, for the third time.

lines: I seem to recall you telling me that the boys were training monkeys to juggle bicycles, and when I came home, there was a stunning lack of monkeys.

expressions.meaning: "There were no monkeys at all." A fancy, funny way to say "zero". "I seem to recall" = I think I remember.
expressions.tone: Sarcastic. Linda is gently making fun of Candace's story.
expressions.example: I opened the cookie jar and found a stunning lack of cookies.
expressions.practice: You get to the beach and there are no waves at all. Say it in a funny way.

toneCards.situation: You open the cookie jar. Nothing.
You arrive at a birthday party, and there's no cake.

expressions.phrase: Aren't you a little young to…? Yes. Yes, I am.

clips.label: Rollercoaster engineer
lines: Candace, seriously, isn't Phineas a little young to be a rollercoaster engineer?
Aren't you a little young to be a rollercoaster engineer?
Well, I must say, I'm very impressed.

clips.label: Fixing Mt. Rushmore
lines: Uh, excuse me, aren't you boys a little young to be restoring a national monument?

expressions.meaning: "Aren't you a little young to…?" = you seem too young for this. Phineas calmly agrees, then does it anyway. This joke comes back in many episodes.
expressions.tone: Phineas is proud and calm, not rude. Repeating "Yes" makes it confident.
expressions.example: "Aren't you a little young to bake a cake by yourself?" "Yes. Yes, I am. Want a slice?"
expressions.practice: A grown-up asks if you're too young to read a really thick book.

toneCards.situation: "Aren't you a little young to bake a cake?"
"Aren't you a little young to climb that wall?" "Yes, I am. Could you help me?"

expressions.phrase: anything at all, just let me know

lines: The forms all seem to be in order, although I've never seen them filled out in crayon before, so if there's anything I can get you, anything at all, just, uh, let me know.
clips.hl: anything at all, just, uh, let me know

expressions.meaning: A polite offer to help. "In order" = correct and complete.
expressions.listen: The joke: an official is being extra polite to a kid who filled in forms with crayon.
expressions.example: If you need anything for the party, anything at all, just let me know.
expressions.practice: A new kid joins your class. Offer to help them.

toneCards.situation: You're helping at the school fair stall.
Your friend is moving house next week.

expressions.meaning: "This is wonderful. I love this." You say it when you're relaxing and happy.
expressions.example: Ice cream, a pool, and no homework. This is the life!
expressions.practice: You're on holiday, lying on a beach chair with a cold drink.

toneCards.situation: You're in a pool on holiday with a cold drink.
You're stuck in a traffic jam in the rain.

clips.label: unexpected → expected
lines: Ah, Perry the Platypus. What an unexpected surprise. And by unexpected, I mean completely expected!
clips.hl: And by unexpected, I mean completely expected!

clips.label: impeccable → peccable
lines: Ah, Perry the Platypus. Your timing is impeccable. And by impeccable, I mean completely peccable!
clips.hl: And by impeccable, I mean completely peccable!

expressions.meaning: People use "And by X, I mean Y" to explain what they really mean. Doofenshmirtz uses it to say the opposite. "Impeccable" = perfect. "Peccable" isn't really used. That's the joke.
expressions.example: My room is a little messy. And by a little, I mean very.
expressions.practice: Describe your sibling's singing using "And by ___, I mean ___."

toneCards.situation: Your little brother "surprises" you, but you saw him hiding.
"I'll be ready in a minute. And by a minute, I mean ten."

lines: You may well ask yourself, why would he do this? What could he possibly have to gain? Well, let me just answer that by saying I haven't really worked out all the bugs yet.

expressions.meaning: "Bugs" = small problems in a plan, machine, or computer game. "Work out" = fix. Joke: Doof doesn't even know why he's doing his plan.
expressions.example: My new game is fun, but I still need to work out a few bugs.
expressions.practice: Your homemade paper rocket keeps crashing. Explain why it's not ready.

toneCards.situation: Show off your robot that "mostly works".
Your robot falls apart in front of the class.

lines: I told you I'm not crazy. I told you.
I see your point, Candace. No crazy person would scream at a post like that. I'll be in the dairy section if you want to come yell at some cheese or anything.

expressions.meaning: Usually: "I understand, and you're right." Here Linda means the opposite: "You just screamed at a post. You are acting crazy."
expressions.tone: Sarcastic. The words agree, but the meaning disagrees. The Fandom script marks Linda as speaking "dryly". The next line, "come yell at some cheese", proves she's joking.
expressions.listen: Sarcasm clue: a calm, flat voice right after something silly happens.
expressions.example: Real: "I see your point. Let's play outside first, then do homework." Sarcastic: your friend trips right after saying "I never fall." You: "I see your point."
expressions.practice: Your friend says, "We should leave early so we don't miss the bus." Agree with them for real.

toneCards.situation: Your friend says, "Let's leave early so we don't miss the bus."
Your brother says, "I never drop things," then drops a plate.
toneCards.note: Means: you just proved yourself wrong.

lines: To fasten, insert the tab into the metal buckle. To release, just pull back on the— Oops. Well, you get the picture. Well, that's about it. Enjoy the ride.

expressions.meaning: "You understand the idea. I don't need to explain more." "That's about it" = that's everything.
expressions.example: Then you add flour, eggs, sugar… you get the picture.
expressions.practice: Start explaining how to brush your teeth, then stop halfway.

toneCards.situation: Explain a game, then skip the boring part.
Pretend to be a parent: "No phones at dinner, no snacks after eight… you get the picture."
toneCards.note: Sounds like rules, not a chat.

expressions.meaning: A calm way to say "that failed". It's funny because his plan failed hugely.
expressions.tone: Understatement: saying something small about something big.
expressions.example: The whole block tower fell over. Well… that didn't work. Try again!
expressions.practice: A wave just washed away your sandcastle.

toneCards.situation: Your huge block tower falls over completely.
toneCards.note: Funny because it's a big failure.

toneCards.situation: Your cake didn't rise at all.

lines: Now, I know I have that club card in here somewhere. I always have it with me, but my purse is such a disaster area. You know how it is.

expressions.meaning: A very messy place. "You know how it is" = this happens to everyone, right?
expressions.example: Don't look under my bed. It's a disaster area.
expressions.practice: Describe your school bag at the end of term.

toneCards.situation: A friend looks inside your school bag.
You open your brother's room door.

expressions.phrase: It's no use! We are doomed!

lines: It's no use! It's no use! We are doomed!
clips.hl: It's no use! It's no use! We are doomed!

expressions.meaning: "It's no use" = trying won't help. "Doomed" = something terrible is sure to happen.
expressions.tone: Dramatic panic. Kids say "We're doomed!" as a joke about small problems.
expressions.example: Five minutes to finish the whole test? We're doomed!
expressions.practice: It starts pouring with rain the minute your picnic begins.

toneCards.situation: Five minutes left to finish the test.
The last zombie wave is coming in your video game.

lines: OK, I give up. What am I supposed to be looking at?

expressions.meaning: "I stop trying to guess. Just tell me."
expressions.tone: Patient but tired.
expressions.example: OK, I give up. What's the answer to the riddle?
expressions.practice: Your teacher asks you a riddle and you can't guess it.

toneCards.situation: Your teacher asks you a riddle you can't solve.
You can't open a jar, no matter how hard you try.

lines: So you think that Phineas and Ferb are still under that stupid tree in the backyard, right?
Well, yes, that would be my guess.
Fine. Then let's go home. Now!

expressions.meaning: "That's what I think." A polite way to answer when you're not 100% sure.
expressions.example: "Is Dad still in the car park?" "That would be my guess."
expressions.practice: Your teacher asks where your missing sock went.

toneCards.situation: "Where's Dad?" "Still at work. That would be my guess."
"Who ate the cake?" Look at your brother's chocolate face.

lines: OK, we're here. Are you happy now, Candace?
Yes! See, Mom? I told you they weren't there.

expressions.plain: Are you happy now? = There. I did what you wanted.
expressions.meaning: "I did what you wanted. Satisfied?" It's not really a question about feelings.
expressions.tone: Annoyed. Be careful: it sounds rude if you say it to a grown-up.
expressions.example: Fine, you can have the last turn. Are you happy now?
expressions.practice: Your sister kept asking you to share the remote. You finally hand it over.

toneCards.situation: Your sister kept nagging, so you finally hand her the remote.
You got your crying cousin's balloon back. "There you go. Happy now?"
toneCards.note: Soft voice: you really want to know.

lines: That was awesome! Can we do it again?

expressions.meaning: "Super cool!" Here "way" = very, very.
expressions.tone: Careful: "way too" usually means too much ("way too hot"). "Way too cool" is slang praise.
expressions.example: Your new scooter is way too cool!
expressions.practice: Your friend shows you a new trick on the monkey bars.

toneCards.situation: Your friend shows you a new trick on the monkey bars.
You jump into the pool: "It's way too cold!"

expressions.phrase: You guys make a great team.

lines: Cool. See you tomorrow. It really was the coolest coaster ever. You guys make a great team.
clips.hl: You guys make a great team.

expressions.meaning: "You work really well together." "You guys" = all of you (boys or girls).
expressions.example: You and your dad make a great team in the kitchen.
expressions.practice: Two classmates built an amazing model together. Tell them.

toneCards.situation: Two classmates built an amazing model together.
Your two friends both drop the same cake.

expressions.phrase: I couldn't have asked for a better one.

lines: Well, a brother is a brother, but I couldn't have asked for a better one than Ferb. You know what I mean?
clips.hl: I couldn't have asked for a better one

expressions.meaning: "He's the best one possible." A warm, sincere compliment.
expressions.listen: Captions say "that Ferb"; he really says "than Ferb".
expressions.example: I couldn't have asked for a better teacher.
expressions.practice: Say thank you to someone who helped you a lot this year.

toneCards.situation: Thank your teacher at the end of the year.
Talk about your pet, or your favorite person.

lines: So what should we do tomorrow? There's a world of possibilities. Maybe we should make a list.

expressions.meaning: "There are so many things we could do."
expressions.example: A whole Saturday with no plans? There's a world of possibilities!
expressions.practice: Plan your next weekend with your teacher. Start big.

toneCards.situation: A whole free Saturday is coming.
A buffet with 100 desserts.

expressions.meaning: "Stop it! You've said that too many times."
expressions.tone: Impatient. Fine with friends, a bit rude to a teacher.
expressions.example: OK, OK, give it a rest. I'll tidy up!
expressions.practice: Your friend keeps asking "Are we there yet?" in the car.

toneCards.situation: Your friend keeps asking, "Are we there yet?"
Your friend keeps worrying about a test that's finished.

lines: Yes! Hey, Ferb! It's Candace's birthday. We've gotta do better than last year.
Not our best work. This time it's gotta be something huge.

expressions.meaning: "We didn't do a good job that time." Honest and a little funny. "Gotta" = have to.
expressions.example: My horse drawing looks like a potato. Not my best work.
expressions.practice: Show your teacher something you made that didn't turn out well.

toneCards.situation: Your horse drawing looks like a potato.
Your drawing is actually great. "Not my best work…"
toneCards.note: You want people to say "It's amazing!"

lines: She's got a big honkin' truckload of ship-launchin' qualities

expressions.meaning: "Big honkin'" = HUGE (silly slang). "Ship-launching" comes from an old story about a woman so beautiful that a thousand ships sailed for her.
expressions.tone: Sung, so use it for meaning, not pronunciation.
expressions.example: I ate a big honkin' slice of pizza.
expressions.practice: Describe the biggest thing you ever ate.

toneCards.situation: Describe the biggest pizza slice you ever ate.
You saw a huge dog at the park.

lines: Candace, and she's anything but ordinary

expressions.meaning: "Anything but X" = definitely NOT X. So she's not ordinary at all; she's special.
expressions.tone: Tricky: it sounds like "anything", but it means "not".
expressions.example: The maths test was anything but easy.
expressions.practice: Describe your best friend using "anything but ___".

toneCards.situation: Describe your best friend: "anything but boring".
"The car trip was anything but relaxing."

lines: Wait. Please don't tell me we're going to Mt. Rushmore.

expressions.meaning: "Oh no, I think something bad is true." You say it when you fear the answer.
expressions.tone: Dread. Funny because her family thinks it's a great surprise.
expressions.example: Please don't tell me we have a spelling test today!
expressions.practice: On Saturday morning, you see Dad carrying the vacuum cleaner toward your room.

toneCards.situation: You see Dad carrying the vacuum toward your room on Saturday.
You see a big LEGO-shaped present. "Please don't tell me…!"
toneCards.note: Here you hope it IS true.

lines: Four American presidents carved into the side of a mountain. It was Phineas' and Ferb's idea.

expressions.meaning: Normally the reply to "thank you". Here Candace didn't say thanks; she glared. Phineas says it anyway.
expressions.tone: Cheeky. Saying "You're welcome" before anyone thanks you is a joke.
expressions.example: I finished the hard part of the puzzle for you. You're welcome.
expressions.practice: You helped your friend without being asked, and they didn't notice.

toneCards.situation: You helped your friend, and they didn't notice.
Your friend says, "Thanks for the pencil!"

lines: OK, you lot go on ahead. I'll find a parking spot and meet you there.

expressions.meaning: "You lot" = British for "you guys". Lawrence (Dad) is British. "Go on ahead" = go first; I'll come later.
expressions.listen: American: "You guys go ahead." British: "You lot go on ahead."
expressions.example: You lot go on ahead. I'll catch up after I tie my shoes.
expressions.practice: Your family is walking to the car, but you need the bathroom first.

toneCards.situation: Tell your family to go ahead to the beach while you park.
"Right, you lot, line up!"

lines: Uh— oh— well, it's my birthday today, and… I… uh… I gotta check something. Back in a flash, OK?

expressions.plain: Back in a flash. = I'll be back very quickly.
expressions.meaning: "I'll be back very quickly."
expressions.tone: Candace is nervous because Jeremy is there. Her "uh… I… uh…" shows it.
expressions.example: Wait here. I'm getting my water bottle. Back in a flash!
expressions.practice: You need to run to your room to get something before you go out.

toneCards.situation: Tell Mom you're getting your water bottle.
You see your crush and suddenly need to leave.

lines: Oh, hi, Isabella. What brings you girls here?

expressions.meaning: A friendly, polite way to ask "Why are you here?"
expressions.example: Hi Uncle Tom! What brings you here?
expressions.practice: You bump into your teacher at the supermarket.

toneCards.situation: You meet your teacher at the supermarket.
You find your friend at the cookie shop, again.

lines: We've just discovered his new hideout is located inside Lincoln's head at Mt. Rushmore. I— I know. You were just there. Poor planning on our part, actually. Sorry.

expressions.meaning: "It's our fault for not planning well."
expressions.example: We forgot the towels at the beach. Poor planning on our part.
expressions.practice: You arrive at the cinema and forgot to buy tickets.

toneCards.situation: Your team forgot the ball for the match.
You went to the beach without a towel.

lines: Mom! Mom, you have got to see this now. Here, look.

expressions.meaning: "There's no time left." The coin telescope stopped just before Mom could look.
expressions.listen: "Oop" is a little sound for a small mistake.
expressions.example: I ran out of time on the last question.
expressions.practice: The game timer ends just before you reach the finish line.

toneCards.situation: The game timer ends just before the finish line.
The quiz timer ends on a question you didn't know.

expressions.phrase: We could use… / You got it!
expressions.meaning: "We could use X" = X would really help us. "You got it!" = Yes, sure, I'll do it!
expressions.listen: Captions put these lines in a different order. This is the order from the Fandom script.
expressions.example: "We could use some help with the bags." "You got it!"
expressions.practice: Your mom says, "We could use someone to set the table."

toneCards.situation: Mom says, "We could use someone to set the table."
Pretend to be a waiter taking an order.

lines: The molten lava of the earth's core completely slipped my mind.

expressions.meaning: "I forgot." Funny: he forgot about the giant hot lava inside the Earth.
expressions.example: Sorry, your birthday card completely slipped my mind!
expressions.practice: You forgot to bring your library book back.

toneCards.situation: You forgot your friend's birthday.
You forgot your shoes when leaving the house.

expressions.phrase: I hate to be a stickler, but…

lines: I hate to be a stickler, but the lava is coming again!
clips.hl: I hate to be a stickler, but

expressions.meaning: A "stickler" cares a lot about rules and small details. "I hate to be a ___, but…" is a polite way to point out a problem.
expressions.tone: Joke: lava coming at you is not a small detail.
expressions.example: I hate to be a stickler, but it's my turn now.
expressions.practice: Your friend just took two turns in a row in a board game.

toneCards.situation: Your friend took two turns in a row.
Remind your teacher that class ends in one minute.

lines: We're running a little behind schedule. Go to Plan B.

expressions.meaning: "Behind schedule" = later than planned. "Plan B" = the backup plan.
expressions.example: It's raining, so Plan B: movie afternoon!
expressions.practice: The park you planned to visit is closed. Tell your friends.

toneCards.situation: The park is closed. "Plan B: let's go to the library."
Your sandcastle is about to be hit by a wave.

expressions.phrase: Some things look better in photos.

lines: You are going to be shocked by what I'm about to show you, Mom.
Hmm. I guess some things look better in photos.
clips.hl: some things look better in photos

expressions.meaning: "In real life, it's less exciting than the pictures." "I guess" = I think (not sure).
expressions.tone: Mildly disappointed, but polite.
expressions.example: The hotel pool is tiny. I guess some things look better in photos.
expressions.practice: A theme park ride looked huge online, but it's small in real life.

toneCards.situation: The theme park ride looked huge online but is tiny.
Your new haircut.

expressions.phrase: the nicest thing anyone has ever done for me

lines: Candace, are you still trying to get the boys in trouble?
No! No, no, this is a great thing. Oh, it's the nicest thing anyone has ever done for me!
clips.hl: the nicest thing anyone has ever done for me

expressions.meaning: A big, sincere thank-you. Candace isn't trying to get her brothers in trouble this time.
expressions.example: You made me a card? That's the nicest thing anyone has ever done for me!
expressions.practice: Your friend made you a surprise birthday drawing.

toneCards.situation: Your friend made you a surprise birthday drawing.
Your brother "kindly" gives you all his chores.

lines: Hurry, Mom. You won't believe it.

expressions.meaning: "It's amazing or very surprising." A great way to start a story.
expressions.example: You won't believe what happened at school today!
expressions.practice: Start telling your teacher about something surprising that happened to you.

toneCards.situation: You scored your first goal.
The class hamster escaped!

lines: Did you like your birthday present?
Well, it was definitely better than the gorilla in the cake.
clips.hl: definitely better than the gorilla in the cake

expressions.meaning: "At least it was better than last time." Ferb (who almost never talks) remembers last year's disaster.
expressions.listen: Ferb is British, like his dad. The Fandom script puts the stress on "definitely".
expressions.example: This year's school play was definitely better than last year's.
expressions.practice: Compare this summer holiday with last summer's.

toneCards.situation: This year's school play vs. last year's.
Your dad's new cooking vs. his burnt pancakes last time.

expressions.phrase: I had a break / I gotta get back.

lines: Hey, Candace, I had a break, and I thought I'd give you this for your birthday. I saw you looking at it in the gift shop.

expressions.meaning: "I had a break" = I had a few free minutes from work. "I gotta get back" = I have to return to work now.
expressions.tone: Funny: Candace said the bobblehead was "lame" before. From Jeremy, she "absolutely loves it".
expressions.example: Nice to see you, but I gotta get back to class.
expressions.practice: Your friend wants to keep chatting, but your swimming lesson is starting.

toneCards.situation: Your swimming lesson is starting.
Break time is over, and you were having fun.

lines: This was the best birthday ever.

clips.label: Rollercoaster: the coolest… ever
lines: Ladies and gentlemen, boys and girls, children of all ages. May I present to you a spectacle most of the morning in the making: the coolest… coaster… ever!

expressions.meaning: "The best ___ ever" = the best of all time. "Ever" at the end makes it stronger.
expressions.listen: Phineas slows down and pauses before "ever" for a big show-host effect.
expressions.example: This was the best holiday ever!
expressions.practice: Tell your teacher about the best day you can remember.

toneCards.situation: The last day of a great holiday.
It rained, you fell over, and you lost your ice cream.
